title: What are custom hooks and when should you extract one?
description: Composing stateful logic across components: naming, rules, common patterns, and when a hook is the wrong tool.

data.text: **Question:** What are custom hooks and when should you extract one?

A custom hook is a function prefixed with `use` that composes other hooks to reuse **stateful logic** — not UI. Each component that calls it gets its own independent copy of the state; the hook shares behavior, not instances. Extract one when the same lifecycle-and-state choreography (subscribing to something, syncing with storage, debouncing an input, managing an async request) appears in two or more components — rule of three is a reasonable bar. Hooks compose better than the old alternatives (HOCs, render props) because there's no wrapper-component nesting or prop drilling of `...props`.

**What a custom hook actually is:**
- Just a function that calls hooks — the `use` prefix is what lets the React Compiler and ESLint rules-of-hooks treat it correctly (conditional-call linting applies inside it)
- State inside is **per-caller**: two components calling `useCart()` see different carts unless they share state through context or a store
- Returns are yours to shape: values, setters, tuples, objects — no restriction
- Can call other custom hooks — layering is the point (`useQuery` → `useDebouncedValue` → `useProducts`)

**Good extraction signals:**
- Same `useState` + `useEffect` choreography in two components (subscribe/unsubscribe, load/cleanup)
- Logic that knows about both React and the outside world: WebSockets, localStorage, media queries, IntersectionObserver, geolocation
- Async request lifecycle: loading/error/data/retry/cancellation — the classic `useFetch`/resource hook
- Timing: debounce (`useDebouncedValue`), throttle, intervals (`useInterval`)

**When NOT to extract:**
- One-time logic in a single component — premature abstraction costs more than duplication
- Pure derivations — that's `useMemo`, not a hook
- UI reuse — that's components; a hook that returns JSX defeats the purpose
- Global client state — that's a store (Zustand/Redux) or context; a hook wrapping a module-level store is fine, but the store is doing the sharing

**Rules that always apply:**
- Call hooks only at the top level of components or other hooks — no loops, conditionals, or early returns before hook calls
- Name it `useX` — ESLint's react-hooks rules and the React Compiler rely on the prefix
- Include a cleanup for every subscription/resource — a leaky hook leaks in every consumer at once

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- Knowing state is per-caller, not shared — the #1 misconception
- The extraction heuristic: repeated stateful choreography, not repeated JSX
- Familiarity with canonical hooks: debounced value, subscription, async resource, media query
- Awareness of the rules-of-hooks constraints and cleanup responsibilities

items: Expecting two components calling the hook to share the same state — they don't
Extracting a hook after the first use (premature abstraction with wrong boundaries)
Skipping cleanup in the hook — now every consumer leaks
Putting conditional logic before hook calls inside the hook body
Wrapping a store in a hook but defining state at module level and calling it 'shared state by hook' without saying so
Naming it without the use prefix — lint rules and the compiler silently stop helping

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Custom hooks reuse stateful logic; each caller gets independent state
Extract when choreography repeats — subscribe, sync, debounce, fetch
use prefix, top-level calls, and cleanup in every effect
UI reuse is components; shared state is stores/context; behavior reuse is hooks
data.takeaway: A custom hook packages 'how this component talks to the world' — extract it when the same conversation repeats, and let each caller keep its own notebook.
